Leurs travaux s’inscrivent dans un corpus croissant de recherches sur les conséquences sociales et politiques des catastrophes liées au climat en Afrique. Il souligne l’importance de répondre aux besoins immédiats des communautés après une catastrophe afin de maintenir l’engagement civique et le soutien du public en faveur d’une adaptation climatique à long terme dans les pays du Sud. Une nouvelle espèce de dinosaure découverte au Zimbabwe Une nouvelle espèce de dinosaure, Musango matusadonaensis, dont les restes ont été découverts près du lac Kariba au Zimbabwe en 2018, apporte un éclairage sur la diversité des animaux qui vivaient dans ce qui est aujourd’hui l’Afrique australe au Trias supérieur, il y a environ 210 millions d’années. Des chercheurs du Royaume-Uni, d’Afrique du Sud et du Zimbabwe ont participé à cette découverte, décrite dans le Journal of Systematic Palaeontology.4 Musango matusadonaensis marchait sur deux pattes, mesurait environ 4,5 mètres de long et pesait, selon les estimations, 220 kilogrammes. Selon l’équipe de recherche, dirigée par Paul Barrett du Musée d’histoire naturelle de Londres, cet animal était nettement plus petit que les sauropodes géants à long cou qui ont évolué par la suite. Il s’agit de la cinquième espèce de dinosaure répertoriée au Zimbabwe. Des découvertes récentes suggèrent que les communautés de dinosaures variaient à travers l’Afrique australe, remettant en cause les hypothèses antérieures selon lesquelles des animaux globalement similaires vivaient dans toute la région. Une étude révèle l’exposition à la dengue chez les enfants des zones côtières du Kenya On sait relativement peu de choses sur la fréquence à laquelle les enfants africains sont exposés au virus de la dengue, l’une des infections virales transmises par les moustiques les plus répandues au monde. Des chercheurs du Programme de recherche du Kenya Medical Research Institute-Wellcome Trust ont examiné les schémas d’exposition sur deux décennies. Leur étude, publiée dans Communications Medicine,5 a mis en évidence une exposition importante au virus de la dengue chez les enfants vivant sur la côte kenyane. L’équipe a analysé 8 025 échantillons sanguins prélevés chaque année entre 1998 et 2018 auprès d’une cohorte de 1 834 enfants âgés de 15 ans et moins. Parmi ces échantillons, 28,5% contenaient des anticorps IgG anti-dengue, indiquant une exposition antérieure au virus. Les anticorps étaient plus fréquents dans les échantillons provenant d’enfants plus âgés. Environ 2% des échantillons prélevés chez des enfants de moins d’un an contenaient des anticorps, contre 40% chez ceux âgés de 9 à 10 ans. La prévalence des anticorps a atteint son pic pendant les années d’épidémie, tandis que le taux le plus élevé de nouvelles infections a été enregistré en 2013, coïncidant avec une importante épidémie sur la côte kenyane. L’étude a examiné son efficacité à l’ère du « traitement universel », où un traitement antirétroviral (TAR) est recommandé pour toute personne chez qui le VIH a été diagnostiqué. Les chercheurs ont analysé les dossiers médicaux électroniques de plus de 235 000 personnes vivant avec le VIH en Haïti, au Kenya, au Nigeria, en Ouganda, au Zimbabwe et en Ukraine. Les données ont été recueillies dans le cadre de l’étude de cohorte prospective intitulée « Programmatic Effectiveness of Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment for People with HIV in Six High-Tuberculosis-Burden Countries » (PROTECT). Selon l’équipe de recherche multinationale, il s’agit de la plus grande évaluation en conditions réelles de l’efficacité du TPT chez les personnes vivant avec le VIH. Dans les six pays étudiés, le fait de commencer le TPT dans les huit semaines suivant l’entrée en prise en charge du VIH a été systématiquement associé à une incidence et à une mortalité plus faibles liées à la tuberculose. By Freda Kreier Freda Kreier View author publications Search author on: PubMed Google Scholar Email Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research People who are infected with dengue virus for a second time often develop severe disease.Credit: Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto via Getty Infecting people with a weak strain of dengue virus is helping researchers to unravel the disease’s bizarre effects on the immune system. Dengue is spread when someone is bitten by an infected female Aedes mosquito. The viral disease kills around 40,000 people every year, with up to 400 million infected annually. Bangladesh and Kenya are among the countries battling a deadly outbreak. Although most adults survive their first brush with the disease, people who are exposed to a second, different strain of dengue virus often develop more severe symptoms. This unusual quirk has complicated dengue vaccine development. Now, a human challenge trial that exposed 45 people to a modified mild strain of dengue virus is beginning to reveal the immunological underpinnings of dengue’s second wind, according to a study published in Science Translational Medicine on 28 October1. Understanding the biology behind dengue’s infection pattern could help researchers to develop better vaccines, says study co-author Leah Katzelnick, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in Bethesda, Maryland. “Dengue is still considered a neglected tropical disease,” she says. “But it’s become a problem for almost everyone now.” Part of the problem with existing dengue vaccines is that even the immunizations can trigger secondary infections. This issue caused concern in the Philippines when some children contracted severe dengue infections after a major public vaccination effort started there in 2016. A dangerous memory Why the secondary infections happen is unclear. One theory is that, when confronted with a different dengue virus strain, the immune system deploys antibodies that were originally generated against the previous dengue strain it encountered. These antibodies aren’t as effective against the second strain, which can lead to people experiencing worse symptoms. Subsequent infections with other variants of dengue don’t seem to trigger the same immune response. To learn more about how dengue immunology works, Katzelnick and her colleagues recruited 45 healthy people and split them into three groups: those who had never been infected with dengue; others who had been infected by one dengue virus strain; and those who had been infected by several dengue strains. The team then exposed all participants to a weakened version of DENV-3 (one of four strains of the virus) and compared their immune responses using blood and lymph-node samples. full_text: A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that’s raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile, Zika and dengue fever. Florida’s struggles with dengue fever in 2026 should be a warning. Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, had seen more than 350 dengue cases, at least one of them fatal, by late October. Miami-Dade County had reported more than 200 cases, and the statewide number was still rising in what has been described as the largest dengue outbreak in modern Florida history. More than 400 of the over 700 Florida cases, including many of those in Hillsborough County and at least seven in the Orlando area, were listed as locally acquired from mosquitoes in the area. Climate change is part of the reason people in many parts of the country are seeing more mosquitoes. Rising global temperatures and shorter winters expand the area suitable for mosquitoes to live in and transmit viruses that cause diseases. Climate change also brings increasingly erratic storm systems, heat and rainfall patterns that leave standing water, creating conditions ideal for mosquitoes to breed. The other major factor shaping where mosquitoes live, often overlooked, is humans themselves. We study entomology and medical geography, including the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. To understand why you may be seeing more mosquitoes, and why communities like Hillsborough County are spending millions of dollars on attempts to control them, start by looking close to home. Mosquitoes follow when humans move in Mosquitoes such as Aedes aegypti – the primary transmitter of pathogens that cause dengue fever, yellow fever, Chikungunya and Zika in the Americas – likely arrived in the U.S. with the slave trade. Both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, a transmitter of many of the same diseases but a more recent arrival in the U.S., are moved by the global shipping network, which can take them to new locations and reintroduce them in parts of their ranges where they may have been controlled in the past. Aedes aegypti’s habits, including its ability to use household environments for living and breeding, have made it a very successful and established invader where climate conditions permit. A flowerpot saucer, clogged gutter, discarded tire, birdbath or even a bottle cap can collect enough water for mosquito larvae to develop. A single Aedes aegypti mosquito can lay more than 100 eggs at a time up to five times during its lifespan, which is only about a month. As suburban neighborhoods expand, so do opportunities for mosquitoes to breed and find humans for their meals. Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people. This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development. Aedes albopictus, originally native to Southeast Asia and now found in all habitable continents, provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes arrived in the U.S. mostly because of human actions. They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo. Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the interstate highway system. By 2017, Aedes albopictus was documented in 1,368 counties across 40 states, and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S. One of Iowa’s first established Aedes albopictus populations, for example, appeared in the Des Moines metropolitan area, where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities. Its spread from southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes. US’s most common mosquito threat: West Nile West Nile virus remains the most widespread mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States. It is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country. Culex mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states. Because Culex mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease. Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus lengthened by an average of 20 days between 1999 and 2024. A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year. In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that Aedes mosquitoes could remain active late into the year. Florida saw a rise in dengue cases. Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial.

Kylee Rae Noel Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people. This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development. A map of Pennsylvania shows where mosquito traps were set (gray) and where Aedes albopictus was discovered from 2010 to 2018. The majority are in heavily populated areas around Philadelphia. Eliza A. H. Little, et al., 2022, CC BY A map of Pennsylvania’s population density in 2020 for comparison. Crossover1370/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY Aedes albopictus, originally native to Southeast Asia and now found in all habitable continents, provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes arrived in the U.S. mostly because of human actions. They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo. Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the interstate highway system. By 2017, Aedes albopictus was documented in 1,368 counties across 40 states, and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S. One of Iowa’s first established Aedes albopictus populations, for example, appeared in the Des Moines metropolitan area, where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities. Its spread from southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes. A 2025 study led by Janey Messina found wide areas likely to be suitable for mosquitoes to transmit dengue by 2050 based on projections of future temperatures, rainfall and mosquito populations. It is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country. Culex mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states. Because Culex mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease. How mosquitoes transmit West Nile virus from birds to humans and other animals. California Department of Public Health Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus lengthened by an average of 20 days between 1999 and 2024. A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year. In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that Aedes mosquitoes could remain active late into the year. Florida saw a rise in dengue cases. Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial. full_text: Murine typhus is a flea-borne rickettsial disease caused by Rickettsia typhi. It presents with nonspecific symptoms and laboratory derangements, which can lead to a delay in diagnosis and treatment. We report the case of a 58-year-old man who presented with fever, altered mental status, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Laboratory testing revealed thrombocytopenia, acute renal failure requiring emergent hemodialysis, transaminitis, and hyperbilirubinemia. An intermediate PLASMIC score initially prompted a concern for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and urgent plasma exchange was initiated after the first round of dialysis, but this was ruled out when ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13) activity was low. During hospitalization, he was newly diagnosed with HIV, with a CD4 count of 65 cells/mm3. Given his fever, he was started on empiric doxycycline for presumed rickettsial infection in the setting of his symptoms, immunocompromised state, and lab abnormalities while confirmatory testing was pending. He completed a 10-day course of doxycycline, was started on antiretroviral therapy, and was discharged after recovery of renal function and resolution of thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, and changes in mental status. This case demonstrates that severe murine typhus can cause multi-organ failure in patients with newly diagnosed HIV/AIDS. Prompt empirical doxycycline, initiated before serologic confirmation, is essential to prevent progression to critical illness. DiscussionMurine typhus is caused by R. typhi, an intracellular gram-negative coccobacillus transmitted to humans by fleas, with rats and opossums serving as amplifying reservoirs rather than vectors [1]. The infection follows a distinct epidemiological pattern, disproportionately affecting urban, port, and coastal regions, including California [1]. It classically presents with a triad of fever, headache, and rash, alongside laboratory findings of elevated liver enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hypoalbuminemia [7,8].The clinical presentation of murine typhus often mimics other acute infectious causes, including scrub typhus, leptospirosis, dengue, and malaria, making a high index of suspicion essential [1]. Our patient's newly diagnosed AIDS, with a CD4 count of 65 cells/mm3, broadened this differential further and prompted an extensive infectious workup that excluded cryptococcosis, coccidioidomycosis, cytomegalovirus infection, and other opportunistic processes. This diagnostic ambiguity took a second, more consequential form: thrombocytopenia with a non-reassuring PLASMIC score for TTP [16], which lead to an initial working diagnosis of TTP and two rounds of empiric plasma exchange before ADAMTS13 activity returned negative, and plasma exchange was discontinued. This case illustrates the central diagnostic challenge: severe murine typhus can present with a laboratory and clinical picture that overlaps substantially with TTP, and distinguishing the two requires ADAMTS13 testing rather than clinical gestalt alone. Even when suspicion shifts toward a rickettsial cause, IgG antibody titers typically are not detectable until 7-10 days after symptom onset, with diagnostic confirmation resting on paired acute- and convalescent-phase titers [17]; therefore, empiric treatment must frequently precede serologic confirmation, as it did here.Several recent case reports have described a similar pattern of murine typhus presenting with multi-organ involvement severe enough to prompt an alternative diagnosis. Wachs and Kuiper [18] reported a case of combined liver and renal failure requiring hemodialysis, with the correct diagnosis reached only after antimicrobial therapy had been empirically narrowed to doxycycline. Pervaiz et al. [19] described murine typhus presenting with DIC and acute psychosis, explicitly noting overlap with TTP-like presentations and recommending early neuroimaging to aid in diagnosis. This presentation, like our patient's altered mental status and intermittent confusion, underscores that neurologic involvement in murine typhus is not incidental; fulminant cases with status epilepticus and other severe neurologic sequelae have been reported [20]. A large recent cohort from Galveston, Texas (149 cases, 2019 through 2023) found that 28% of hospitalized patients required intensive care and that both deaths in the cohort involved multi-organ failure complicated by hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis [13], a reminder that severe murine typhus, independent of any comorbidity, carries a real risk of critical illness.What distinguishes our case was the specific mechanism of diagnostic confusion: to our knowledge, this is among the more detailed accounts of murine typhus triggering a full TTP workup, including a validated pretest probability score and two rounds of plasma exchange, before ADAMTS13 testing redirected the diagnosis in a patient whose presentation ultimately spanned five organ systems: hematologic (thrombocytopenia), renal (acute kidney injury), hepatic (transaminitis), gastrointestinal (ileus), and neurologic (altered mental status and confusion). This combination, not the patient's HIV status per se, is what made this case diagnostically instructive and is the primary contribution we believe this report makes to the literature.The pathogenesis of R. typhi centers on microvascular endothelial injury and vasculitis [1,5,6], resulting in increased vascular permeability, capillary leakage, and platelet consumption with microthrombi formation [6,21-23]. This microangiopathic process can manifest as kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, petechiae, or hepatic dysfunction [6,21,22]. In the renal system, this injury can result in prerenal azotemia, acute tubular necrosis, and, rarely, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, as described in a previous murine typhus case report [5]. Within the gastrointestinal system, intestinal microvascular dysfunction and mucosal hypoperfusion can produce bowel wall edema, impaired motility, and ileus in severe infections [7,24,25], as occurred in our patient on hospital day 7, manifesting as tachycardia and requiring nasogastric decompression and neostigmine.The severity of rickettsial infection depends, in part, on host factors; fatal outcomes have been associated with older or male adults and patients with diabetes, alcohol use disorder, or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency [26]. Whether HIV/AIDS independently worsens murine typhus severity has not been established. A serosurvey of HIV-infected patients found R. typhi seroprevalence and clinical correlates similar to the general population [12], and a large case series characterizing complications of murine typhus explicitly excluded patients with untreated HIV infection from the analysis, alongside other confounding diagnoses [4], leaving this population understudied rather than demonstrating worse outcomes. The newly diagnosed AIDS broadened the initial differential diagnosis and likely contributed to the decision to pursue an aggressive infectious workup. However, the TTP-mimicking presentation and its resolution with doxycycline rather than plasma exchange are the features that make this case worth reporting, independent of the patient’s immunological status.Doxycycline remains the cornerstone of therapy for murine typhus [27], and early empiric treatment, often initiated before confirmatory testing, as in the case reports above and in ours, is critical for reducing morbidity and mortality [1,13]. Within days of starting doxycycline, our patient improved: renal function normalized, the ileus resolved, thrombocytopenia resolved, mentation cleared, and no further intervention was required.As a single case, this report is illustrative and hypothesis-generating rather than generalizable; it cannot establish causality between HIV/AIDS and murine typhus severity, and the absence of a convalescent-phase serology sample limits definitive confirmation of the diagnosis beyond a single elevated acute-phase titer. ConclusionsThis case illustrates that severe murine typhus can closely mimic TMAs (TTP/HUS), presenting with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. This presentation spanned five organ systems, underscoring that murine typhus can produce diffuse multisystem injury independent of any comorbidity.Clinicians evaluating undifferentiated febrile illness with thrombocytopenia and multi-organ involvement should consider murine typhus in the differential diagnosis. The differential for fever with thrombocytopenia and multi-organ involvement is broad and extends well beyond TMA. Non-infectious mimics include hemolytic uremic syndrome and systemic autoimmune disease, while infectious mimics include leptospirosis, dengue, ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis, acute HIV, acute viral hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus infection, secondary syphilis, and disseminated gonococcal infection. Many were pursued with directed serologic, molecular, and culture testing in this patient, and none of the overlapping clinical features separated R. typhi from its mimics at the bedside. In our patient, a newly diagnosed HIV infection broadened the initial infectious workup but was not established as the reason for his severe presentation. Prompt empirical doxycycline, initiated before serologic confirmation, is essential to prevent progression to critical illness. IntroductionMurine typhus is an infection caused by Rickettsia typhi, which is transmitted to humans via the bite of infected fleas, with rats and opossums serving as amplifying reservoirs rather than vectors [1]. It exhibits a distinct epidemiological pattern, commonly affecting urban, port, and coastal regions, including California [1]. Although historically regarded as uncommon, murine typhus is a reemerging disease in the United States, with cases concentrated in warm coastal areas of California and Texas [2]. Reported cases in Los Angeles County have risen steadily since 2010, reaching 171 in 2022, the year of the most recent local fatality cluster [3]. Its true incidence is likely underestimated because the presentation is nonspecific and flea exposure is frequently unrecognized by patients [4].Rickettsial infection targets vascular endothelial cells, leading to microvascular injury, tissue hypoperfusion, and microthrombus formation [1,5,6]. In immunocompetent hosts, murine typhus classically presents with a triad of fever, headache, and maculopapular rash that begins on the trunk and spreads to the extremities, sparing the palms and soles [7,8]. However, this triad is present in only about one-third of patients, and the diagnosis more often rests on a recognizable but nonspecific laboratory signature: a tetrad of elevated hepatic transaminases, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hypoalbuminemia, frequently accompanied by thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia [4,7]. This constellation overlaps substantially with sepsis and with the thrombocytopenia and organ injury of a thrombotic microangiopathy.This presentation can be difficult to distinguish from other causes of thrombocytopenia and multi-organ dysfunction, including thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic organ injury defines the thrombotic microangiopathies (TMAs), a group that extends well beyond TTP to include Shiga-toxin-mediated and complement-mediated (atypical) hemolytic uremic syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), drug-induced TMA, malignancy, pregnancy-associated TMA, and autoimmune disease [9,10]. Systemic infection is a particularly important and under-recognized TTP mimic: a systematic review of infection-associated TTP/HUS-like presentations identified 41 distinct infectious etiologies, including cytomegalovirus, HIV, ehrlichiosis, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), organisms that, like R. typhi, injure the vascular endothelium [11]. Other infectious causes of an acute febrile, thrombocytopenic, multi-organ illness relevant to this setting include leptospirosis, dengue, and other rickettsioses [7].Data on murine typhus in people with HIV are limited. A serosurvey of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected patients found R. typhi seroprevalence and clinical correlates comparable to the general population, with no association with CD4 count or CDC stage [12]. Large clinical series characterizing severe murine typhus have generally comprised immunocompetent patients or explicitly excluded untreated HIV infection, and, thus, whether advanced HIV/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) independently worsens severity, produces atypical presentations, or increases complications has not been established [4,13].This case describes a severe manifestation of murine typhus that closely mimicked TTP in a patient with newly diagnosed AIDS. In this patient, the pivot from TTP to murine typhus rested on two steps. First, TTP was effectively excluded: severe (<10%) ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13) deficiency is specific for TTP, whereas the mild-to-moderate reductions seen in sepsis, DIC, liver disease, and other secondary TMAs are not [14,15]; our patient's ADAMTS13 activity was low but not severely deficient (0.51 IU/mL), making TTP unlikely and prompting discontinuation of plasma exchange. Second, once a primary TMA was excluded, the combination of fever, transaminitis, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and newly recognized advanced HIV in a resident of an endemic coastal region redirected attention to a rickettsial and opportunistic-infection differential, prompting empiric doxycycline and confirmatory R. typhi serology.This case was previously presented as a poster at the Solomon Scholars Internal Medicine Conference at the University of California, Los Angeles on May 18, 2026. Case presentationA 58-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea. He worked as a butcher and landscaper, lived in Los Angeles, California, and reported engaging in sexual activity with men. He denied recent travel, known allergies, prescribed or over-the-counter medications, or substance use. On presentation, he was febrile (38.3°C), tachycardic (heart rate of 101 beats per minute), and tachypneic (respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute), and had a blood pressure of 128/69 mmHg. This constellation overlaps substantially with sepsis and with the thrombocytopenia and organ injury of a thrombotic microangiopathy.This presentation can be difficult to distinguish from other causes of thrombocytopenia and multi-organ dysfunction, including thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Systemic infection is a particularly important and under-recognized TTP mimic: a systematic review of infection-associated TTP/HUS-like presentations identified 41 distinct infectious etiologies, including cytomegalovirus, HIV, ehrlichiosis, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), organisms that, like R. typhi, injure the vascular endothelium [11]. A serosurvey of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected patients found R. typhi seroprevalence and clinical correlates comparable to the general population, with no association with CD4 count or CDC stage [12]. title: Climate-Pollution-Pathogen Based Systems Model of Environmental Drivers of Infectious Disease Emergence Across Urban and Peri-Urban Bangladesh
abstract: Infectious disease emergence in Bangladesh reflects converging climatic, pollution, sanitation, and biological pressures across rapidly urbanizing landscapes, yet these drivers are rarely examined within a unified mediation framework. The study harmonized national epidemiological data with a 720 site-month panel from 30 urban and peri-urban sites across six metropolitan areas. Model-derived pathogen burden and incidence were generated mathematically from published exposure-response relationships. Negative-binomial regression, interaction testing, stratified models, restricted cubic splines, and structural equation modeling were applied. Reported dengue cases increased from 5,521 in 2000 and 101,354 in 2019 to 321,179 in 2023, before declining to 101,214 in 2024. Mean temperature was 27.4°C, PM2.5 62.7 μg/m3, and NO2 38.6 μg/m3. Incidence increased 9% per °C (IRR=1.09, 95% CI 1.05-1.13), 6% per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 (IRR=1.06, 1.03-1.09), and 48% with pathogen positivity (IRR=1.48, 1.28-1.71). Temperature–PM2.5 interaction was significant (IRR=1.04, 1.01-1.07). Structural modeling showed acceptable fit and identified pathogen burden as the strongest direct determinant (β=0.43). Climate change, particulate pollution, and pathogen burden interact with each other rather than act independently, with stronger temperature effects in urban settings. Integrated surveillance incorporating environmental pathogen indicators alongside climate and clinical data may better capture disease emergence pathways in further research.

Keywords: climate change; ambient particulate matter; dengue; infectious disease emergence; peri-urban; mediation analysis; One Health; Bangladesh 1. Introduction Bangladesh is among the most densely settled, the most climatically exposed, polluted, and rapidly urbanizing nations in the world. Each of those facts is separately well known. What is less often stated is that they are simultaneously true of the same 170 million people living in the same deltaic space, which is why the country has become an unusually legible natural experiment in how environmental stressors combine. The exposures do not queue up and wait their turn. Rainfall creates larval habitat. Particulate matter degrades respiratory defense and raises the risk of lower respiratory tract infection. Inadequate sanitation and unregulated industrial discharge put enteric and resistant organisms into the water that households drink and store. Land conversion for urbanization removes the drainage and vegetation that would otherwise buffer both flooding and heat. What results is a transmission surface on which several pathogen classes become more likely at once, and on which the marginal effect of any single driver depends on how much of the others is present. Dengue was first detected in what is now Bangladesh in 1966, and the first major outbreak arrived with the monsoon of 2000, producing 5,521 officially reported cases and 93 deaths (Al‐Amin et al., 2020). Nineteen years later the 2019 outbreak reached 101,354 confirmed cases and 164 deaths. By 2023 the country recorded 321,179 cases and 1,705 deaths, a burden 1.3 times the 244,246 cases of the preceding 23 years and a death toll twice the 849 fatalities recorded across 2000 to 2022 (Hasan et al., 2025). A further 101,214 cases were reported in 2024 (Shiddik et al., 2026). The geography moved with the numbers: during the 2019 outbreak 48.4 percent of cases were reported from all 64 districts, and one least developed district town urbanized by more than 600 percent within two decades (Hossain et al., 2023). Dengue is the only prevalent disease in this country. Near-annual Nipah virus outbreaks have occurred since 2001, with case fatality reaching 90 percent in some outbreaks and 322 infections identified nationally by 2021 (Satter et al., 2023; Wit et al., 2014). Approximately 30 emerging viral diseases have been documented globally in recent decades, and roughly 70 percent are zoonotic in origin (Samad, 2025). Few countries have absorbed as much of that burden as Bangladesh, which has reported highly pathogenic avian influenza, Nipah, pandemic H1N1, and COVID-19 since 2001 (Chowdhury et al., 2021). The intellectual trajectory here has been away from single-cause accounts. Land use change, including agricultural encroachment, deforestation, road construction, dam building, irrigation, wetland modification, and the concentration or expansion of urban environments, drives a cascade of secondary factors that exacerbate emergence, among them forest fragmentation, pathogen introduction, pollution, poverty, and human migration (Patz et al., 2004). Urbanization creates diverse wildlife-livestock-human interfaces where anthropogenic pressures generate critical points for cross-species transmission (Rulli et al., 2025). Extended urbanization, the outward expansion of metropolitan influence into suburban and peri-urban zones, raises vulnerability through three recurring mechanisms: demographic change, infrastructure, and governance (Connolly et al., 2020). Peri-urban space is the critical and least governed component of this system. It is typically under- governed, undergoing rapid environmental change, and highly susceptible to zoonotic transfer, and it abuts dense urban populations, creating pathways through which emerging pathogens reach large susceptible populations (Matthew et al., 2021). Bangladeshi demography sharpens the point: the country will be majority urban by approximately 2039, and slum populations within cities are growing at approximately double the average urban rate (Ángeles et al., 2018; Streatfield & Ahsan, 2009). This study treats that frontier as a coupled system rather than a set of parallel risks. It specifies four interacting subsystems (hydroclimatic drivers, environmental contamination, exposure and vulnerability, and pathogen amplification), derives pathogen burden and incidence mathematically from documented exposure-response relations, estimates conditional and mediated relationships among the subsystems on a harmonized multi-site panel, and tests whether the exposure-disease relationship is modified by position along the urban-to-peri-urban gradient. 2. Literature Review The conceptual foundation for integrating climate, pollution, pathogens, and society lies in coupled human and natural systems. Systems integration links socioeconomic and environmental components through frameworks incorporating ecosystem services, planetary boundaries, human- nature nexuses, and telecoupling, while facing challenges in quantifying spillovers, feedbacks, and cross-scale interactions (Liu et al., 2015). Telecoupling captures interactions across distances and evolved into metacoupling to track flows of matter, energy, information, organisms, and capital (Liu, 2017; Liu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018). Infectious disease was subsequently incorporated into these systems models spanning health risks, habitat change, and institutional conditions, where climate change and peri-urban expansion interact to create socio-ecological conditions conducive to zoonotic transmission and health vulnerability (Gibb et al., 2025). Two methodological strands strengthen this systems view. Environmental epidemiology provides mechanisms through which vegetation modifies infection risks such as higher greenness (NDVI) being associated with reduced influenza odds (Cai et al., 2025), lower COVID-19 severe disease prevalence mediated by NO2 (Peng et al., 2022), and reduced neighborhood infection rates (Spotswood et al., 2021). Distributed lag nonlinear models (DLNMs) complement this by specifying joint functions for predictor and lag dimensions to capture delayed exposure-response relationships, with direct application to early warning systems (Lowe et al., 2018). Bangladesh's urban transition is characterized by rapid population redistribution toward settlements with limited infrastructure. Dhaka rose to an expansive megacity of over 17 million inhabitants, with future growth expected to make the country predominantly urban by 2039 (Rashid, 2009). Epidemiologically, growth is heavily concentrated in slums and informal settlements, which grow at twice the average urban rate and accommodate millions of migrants (Hossain, 2014; Shafique et al., 2018). Driven by economic opportunities and coastal climate displacement, migration fuels peri-urban expansion where socio- material transformations, expanded livestock production, and governance gaps heighten zoonotic, foodborne, and waterborne disease risks at the metropolitan edge (Aggarwal et al., 2020; Dorsey, 2024; Gras, 2024). The climate-disease relationship in Dhaka is distinctly non-linear and delayed. While monsoon rainfall exhibits threshold-dependent associations with disease vectors where rainfall above 70 mm significantly increases case risks across extended lags (Hashizume et al., 2012), seasonal thermal envelopes (26-30°C) and high humidity sustain hyperendemic dengue transmission (Faruk, 2026). Recent nationwide surges have demonstrated expanded geographic reach across all 64 districts, rising case-fatality rates, shifting serotype dominance (DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4), and severe clinical burdens (Asaduzzaman et al., 2025; Billah et al., 2025; Debnath et al., 2025; Ogieuhi et al., 2025). Future CMIP6 climate projections indicate substantial further increases in precipitation and temperatures across all SSP scenarios, compounding long-term vector-borne risk (Almazroui et al., 2020; Bhattacharjee et al., 2023; Kamruzzaman et al., 2023). Environmental pressures are heavily amplified by air and water pollution across urban environments. Bangladesh and Dhaka consistently rank among the world's most polluted regions (Hossain et al., 2025), where winter particulate levels( PM 10 and PM 2.5) reach two to three times national standards due to combustion sources like brick kilns, vehicles, and industry (Afrin et al., 2020; Ahmed et al., 2024; Majumder et al., 2026). Exceeding WHO guidelines directly increases respiratory infections, wet coughs, and thousands of premature deaths, generating massive GDP losses (Bangladesh & Hossain, 2019). Concurrently, in informal settlements, unpurified water use, shared latrines, and inconsistent handwashing drive high rates of pediatric communicable and diarrheal diseases (Biswas et al., 2026; Farzana et al., 2024; Sayda et al., 2025), though targeted hygiene interventions prove highly protective (Ejemot-Nwadiaro et al., 2015; Fewtrell et al., 2004; Shahid et al., 1996; Stanton & Clemens, 1987) and green space buffers acute pediatric infections (Zhang et al., 2024). Industrial discharges including thousands of tons of untreated tannery and dyeing waste into the Buriganga River further degrade regional aquatic ecosystems (Hossain et al., 2021; Mustari & Afsana, 2021; Rahman et al., 2020; Rampley et al., 2019; Sathi, 2023). These exposures translate into disease through complex vector and biological pathways. Unreliable piped water forces household water storage, creating primary Aedes breeding sites (Ferdousi et al., 2015), while chemical vector control is constrained by evolving insecticide resistance (Deming et al., 2016; Maciel-de-Freitas et al., 2014; Marcombe et al., 2018). Zoonotic transmission presents another major threat: Nipah virus repeatedly spills over via raw date-palm sap consumption (Gurley et al., 2017; Islam et al., 2016; Khan et al., 2012), while avian influenza (H5N1), swine flu, chikungunya, and Zika virus pose ongoing re-emerging risks driven by land-use change, deforestation, and agricultural intensification (Chowdhury et al., 2021; Ferdous et al., 2026; Hasan et al., 2025; Khatun et al., 2015; Murray & Daszak, 2013; Rohr et al., 2019; Samad, 2013, 2025). Finally, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) operates across this same human-animal-environment continuum. Multidrug-resistant bacteria, beta-lactamase, and colistin-resistance genes are widely documented across livestock, wildlife, hospital waste, and urban insect vectors (Akter et al., 2020; Cook et al., 2025; Iskandar et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2020; Parvez et al., 2016; Rahman et al., 2026; Sharif et al., 2025). Mitigating these intersecting challenges requires establishing cross-sectoral One Health surveillance and genomic frameworks to guide environmental governance and infection prevention (Hassan et al., 2021; Singh & Mitra, 2026). 3. Research Gap The demographic and spatial transformation of urban Bangladesh is thoroughly documented, including peri-urban settlement growth and urban slum expansion at roughly double the average urban rate. The hydroclimatic epidemiology of dengue is comparatively precise, with a rainfall threshold of 70 mm and a 29.0 percent case increase per 10 mm above threshold at lags of 0 to 19 weeks. Air pollution burdens are quantified at national scale alongside exposure-response functions for respiratory outcomes. Zoonotic spillovers and antimicrobial resistance have been characterized as interface phenomena. And the coupled human and natural systems tradition provides the architecture within which such phenomena can be integrated. Yet the dengue modelers rarely enter air quality into their specifications, pollution assessments treat infectious outcomes as a secondary category, sanitation research is framed around diarrheal disease and nutrition, and resistance research is almost never linked to the environmental change processes driving urbanization. Peri-urban space suffers from a different neglect. The Bangladeshi urban health literature concentrates on Dhaka, even though peripheral districts and secondary towns now record rising incidence and 48.4 percent of cases in the 2019 outbreak came from all 64 districts. Comparative estimation across the urban gradient is therefore nearly absent, because existing studies sample one setting or one city rather than assembling climatic, air quality, land cover, sanitation, and outcome data on a common framework. And no study has yet specified coupled subsystems with defined transmission pathways and then tested the resulting structure using indirect-effect estimation. 4. Research Objectives General objective: To develop and apply a systems model of the climate-pollution-pathogen nexus that explains how coupled environmental drivers shape infectious disease emergence in urban and peri-urban Bangladesh, and to test the model against a harmonized multi-site panel. Specific objectives: 1. To characterize national trends and geographic distributions of emerging infectious diseases using surveillance aggregates and published secondary data. 2. To quantify hydroclimatic associations, nonlinear thresholds, and lagged effects on infectious disease transmission using distributed lag and time-series models. 3. To assess ambient pollution as an environmental susceptibility modifier by quantifying pollutant concentrations relative to national standards and estimating interaction effects with climatic exposures. 4. To test the integrated climate–pollution–pathogen nexus by examining mediation pathways and differences in exposure–disease associations between urban and peri-urban settings, thereby identifying implications for surveillance, regulation, and environmental health governance in Bangladesh. 5. Methodology 5.1 Design logic and estimation sequence This study is an observational analytical design integrating national descriptive epidemiology with a multi-site panel and a systems model test. The study began with compilation and harmonization of the environmental layers, moved through descriptive and threshold characterization, then unadjusted estimation, then adjusted estimation with product terms, then stratified estimation across settlement types, then nonlinear dose-response modeling, and finally mediation estimation through a structural equation model. Systems integration links socioeconomic and environmental components through frameworks incorporating ecosystem services, planetary boundaries, human- nature nexuses, and telecoupling, while facing challenges in quantifying spillovers, feedbacks, and cross-scale interactions (Liu et al., 2015). Telecoupling captures interactions across distances and evolved into metacoupling to track flows of matter, energy, information, organisms, and capital (Liu, 2017; Liu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018). Infectious disease was subsequently incorporated into these systems models spanning health risks, habitat change, and institutional conditions, where climate change and peri-urban expansion interact to create socio-ecological conditions conducive to zoonotic transmission and health vulnerability (Gibb et al., 2025).
